docs.x: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution. An agent is Claude in a loop. Your code sends the conversation, reads stop_reason, runs the tools Claude asked for, appends the results and repeats until Claude ends its turn.

The Messages API is stateless. Claude never runs a tool itself and never remembers the last call. An agentic loop is the code you write around the API that makes repeated calls look like one autonomous piece of work. Each pass through the loop does four things: 1. Send the full conversation so far, with the tool definitions, to Claude. 2. Inspect stop_reason on the response. 3. If it is "tool_use" , execute every tool Claude requested, in your code. 4. Append Claude's response and a tool_result for each tool call to the history, then go back to step 1. When stop_reason is "end_turn" , Claude has finished and the loop stops. messages = [{"role": "user", "content": request}] while True: response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=4096, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content}) if response.stop_reason != "tool_use": break # end_turn, or a case handled below results = [] for block in response.content: if block.type == "tool_use": output = run_tool(block.name, block.input) results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": output}) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results}) Two details carry marks in the exam. Each tool_result must carry the tool_use_id of the call it answers, and the results go back in a user message. That is the only way the model sees what a tool returned.

"tool_use" and "end_turn" are the two that drive the loop, but a robust harness handles the others explicitly rather than treating them as success. stop_reason Meaning Typical handling end_turn Claude finished its turn Stop; use the final response tool_use Claude wants one or more tools run Run them, append results, continue max_tokens Output hit the token limit mid-response Treat as incomplete: continue or raise the limit, never present it as done stop_sequence A configured stop sequence was emitted Treat like an end of turn unless that sequence has a special meaning for you The Agent SDK runs this loop for you. You still need to understand it, because the SDK's turn limits, budgets and hooks all attach to these same steps.

docs.c: Let stop_reason end the loop · Anti-patterns the exam offers as answers · A refund lookup, step by step
docs.x: In an agentic loop Claude decides which tool to call next, based on what earlier results showed. That is different from a pre-configured decision tree or a fixed sequence of tool calls written in your code. The model-driven loop handles cases nobody scripted; a fixed sequence is cheaper and more predictable when the steps never change (lesson 1.6 covers that choice). The loop continues while stop_reason is "tool_use" and stops when it is "end_turn" . Everything else is a safeguard, not the stopping rule. - Parsing Claude's text for phrases like "I'm done" or "issue resolved" to decide when to stop. - Stopping when the response contains any text. Claude often writes text and requests a tool in the same response. - An iteration cap (for example, stop after 10 calls) as the primary stopping mechanism. A cap is a sensible safety net against runaway loops, but it cuts off legitimate long tasks and lets nothing finish on its own terms. - Assuming the API or an MCP server feeds tool results to the model automatically. A customer asks about a late order. Claude's first response requests get_customer (stop_reason tool_use ). The harness runs it and appends the result. Claude then requests lookup_order ; the harness runs that too. On the third call Claude writes a reply to the customer and stops with end_turn . Nothing in the harness decided the order of those calls: Claude chose each one from what the previous result showed.

Expect a harness with one flaw. Common ones: the loop stops on text content; it stops after a fixed number of iterations; tool results are not appended, so Claude repeats the same call; a max_tokens response is shown to the customer as a finished answer. Pick the option that makes stop_reason the control signal and keeps the history complete.

Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns. In a hub-and-spoke system the coordinator decomposes the work, decides which subagents a query actually needs, routes every message, and loops back when the synthesis has gaps.

In a coordinator-subagent (hub-and-spoke) system, one coordinator agent sits at the centre and specialised subagents sit at the spokes. The coordinator owns four jobs: 1. Decompose the request into pieces of work. 2. Delegate each piece to the right subagent. 3. Aggregate what comes back into one result. 4. Decide which subagents a given request needs at all. Subagents do not talk to each other. Every message goes through the coordinator, which gives you one place for logging, error handling and control over what information flows where.

docs.h: Subagents start with a clean context
docs.x: A subagent does not inherit the coordinator's conversation history. It sees its own system prompt and whatever the coordinator puts in the task it hands over, nothing more. Lesson 1.3 covers how to pass context; here the point is architectural: if the synthesis subagent needs the search findings, the coordinator must send them.

docs.h: Match the pipeline to the query
docs.x: A coordinator that always runs every subagent wastes time and money. "When did the regulation take effect?" needs one search, not search plus document analysis plus synthesis plus a formatted report. A good coordinator analyses the query first and invokes only the subagents it needs: one for a simple fact, the full pipeline for a broad research question.

docs.h: Decomposition can fail by being too narrow
docs.x: The commonest quality failure in research systems is not a bad subagent but a narrow decomposition . Asked about "AI in creative industries", a coordinator that splits the work into digital art, graphic design and photography never asks anyone about music, film or writing. Every subagent does its job well and the report is still incomplete. The fix is at the coordinator: a broader decomposition, and a review of coverage before the report is written.

When several subagents search in parallel, give each a distinct slice : separate subtopics, separate source types, separate time ranges. Overlapping assignments burn tokens finding the same sources twice. Where topics genuinely intersect, assign the overlap to one subagent deliberately and deduplicate at synthesis.

docs.c: The coordinator is the only hub · Fixing the wrong layer · Always running the full pipeline · One question, two paths
docs.x: A single pass rarely produces complete coverage. The stronger design is an iterative refinement loop : 1. Subagents research; synthesis produces a draft. 2. The coordinator evaluates the draft against the question: which subtopics are thin or missing? 3. It re-delegates targeted queries for those gaps to the search and analysis subagents. 4. Synthesis runs again with the new findings. Repeat until coverage meets the bar. Decomposition, routing, error handling and the decision to loop again all live in the coordinator. If subagents start messaging each other directly, you lose the single point of observability. When a report misses whole subtopics, options that tune the search subagent or the synthesis prompt are tempting. If the subtopics were never assigned, the defect is the coordinator's decomposition. "Invoke every subagent so nothing is missed" sounds thorough. It is the anti-pattern: the coordinator should select subagents from what the query needs. "What was the EU's 2025 battery recycling target?" The coordinator sends one search task and returns the answer with its source. "How will the battery regulation change the European e-bike market over five years?" The coordinator splits the work into regulation, supply chain, pricing and demand; sends search and document tasks in parallel; reviews the draft; finds pricing thin; re-delegates two pricing queries; then runs synthesis and the report.

Scenario 3 (multi-agent research) is the natural home for these questions. Look for: subagents communicating directly, a coordinator that always runs everything, a report with whole missing subtopics, duplicated work across subagents, or a single-pass design with no gap check. The right answer usually changes the coordinator's behaviour.

Whitfield's coordinator runs all four subagents for every question and produces reports with missing subtopics. Write the coordinator's operating rules. 1. Write a routing rule. Say how the coordinator decides between a single search and the full pipeline, with one example of each. 2. Write the decomposition step. For the question "How will EU battery regulation affect the e-bike market?", list the slices you would assign and how you keep them from overlapping. 3. Add the gap loop. Describe what the coordinator checks in a draft, what it does when a subtopic is thin, and when it stops. Done when: the loop has a stopping condition that is about coverage, not a fixed number of rounds. 4. State the communication rule between subagents. 1. Routing. The coordinator first classifies the question. A lookup (one fact, one date, one number) gets a single web search task and a short answer with its source. A research question (trends, comparisons, forecasts) gets the full pipeline. Example lookup: "When did the EU battery regulation enter into force?" Example research: "How will it affect e-bike makers' costs to 2030?" 2. Decomposition Slice Subagent Sources What the regulation requires and when Web search Official texts and regulator summaries Supply chain and recycling capacity Web search Industry bodies and news, last 24 months Pricing and margins Document analysis Client-supplied cost data Demand and market size Web search Market studies, with publication dates Each slice is defined by subtopic and source type, so two subagents should not be reading the same pages. Recycling costs touch both the supply chain and pricing slices; it is assigned to supply chain only, and synthesis merges duplicates. 3. Gap loop. After each draft the coordinator lists the question's subtopics and marks each as covered (two or more independent sources), thin (one source) or missing. For each thin or missing subtopic it sends one targeted query to the right subagent, then re-runs synthesis. It stops when every subtopic is covered or when a subtopic has been retried twice without new sources, in which case the gap goes into the report's coverage section. 4. Communication. Subagents never message each other. Everything they produce returns to the coordinator, which decides what each next task receives. - My routing rule makes the coordinator choose subagents per question. - My slices differ by subtopic or source type. - My loop stops on coverage, and reports gaps it cannot close. - All traffic goes through the coordinator.

Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning. Subagents are spawned through the Task tool, start with no memory of the coordinator's conversation, and only know what you put in their prompt, so pass complete findings, keep metadata structured, and spawn in parallel.
What you need to know

docs.c: The tool's new name is Agent
docs.x: A coordinator spawns a subagent by calling a tool : the Task tool. Two consequences follow: - If the coordinator's allowedTools does not include "Task" , it cannot delegate , however clearly its system prompt tells it to. It will do the work itself. - Spawning is a tool call like any other, so it shows up in the loop and in hooks. The exam guide uses the name Task , so answer exam questions with Task. In current Agent SDK and Claude Code releases the same tool is named Agent : it appears as Agent in tool_use blocks and is listed as Agent in allowed_tools . Older releases, and the session's tool list, still show Task . The behaviour is identical.

Each subagent type is described by an AgentDefinition : Field Purpose description Tells the coordinator when to use this subagent prompt The subagent's own system prompt tools The tools this subagent may use, restricted to its role model Optional model override options = ClaudeAgentOptions( allowed_tools=["Task", "Read", "Grep"], # "Agent" in current releases agents={ "synthesis": AgentDefinition( description="Combines research findings into a structured draft.", prompt="You merge findings. Keep every claim's source.", tools=["Read"], ), }, )

docs.h: Subagents inherit nothing you do not pass
docs.x: A non-forked subagent starts with a fresh context . It does not receive the coordinator's conversation history, earlier tool results, or another subagent's output, and nothing is shared between one invocation and the next. The only bridge is the prompt the coordinator writes for it. So when the synthesis subagent writes a generic report that cites none of the search results, the likeliest cause is simple: nobody put the search results in its prompt .

docs.h: What to put in a subagent's prompt
docs.x: - Complete findings from earlier agents , not a one-line paraphrase. The synthesis subagent needs the search results and document analysis themselves. - Structure that separates content from metadata , so attribution survives: each finding with its source URL or document name, page, and date. - The goal and quality criteria , not a script. "Find evidence on recycling capacity in the EU since 2023; prefer primary sources; flag conflicts" lets the subagent adapt. "Run these five queries in order and summarise the top three results" breaks the moment the topic does not fit the script. {"findings": [ {"claim": "EU recycling capacity grew 40% in 2024", "source": "https://example.org/report-2025", "page": 12, "published": "2025-03-10"} ]}

To run independent subagents at the same time, the coordinator emits several Task calls in one response . Emitting one per turn makes them run one after another: two tasks of 15 and 20 seconds take 35 seconds in sequence and about 20 in parallel.

docs.c: If the subagent needs it, put it in the prompt · "The prompt says to delegate" · Procedural scripts for subagents
docs.x: For exploring two divergent approaches from the same analysis, a fork copies the conversation so far into a new, independent branch (lesson 1.7). A fork is the exception to "starts fresh": it inherits the history up to the fork point. Context isolation is the default. Every fact, file path, finding and constraint a subagent needs must be written into its task. A coordinator that ignores delegation instructions is often missing the Task tool in allowedTools . No amount of prompt wording fixes a missing tool. Step-by-step query lists look controlled but make subagents brittle. The exam prefers goals plus quality criteria.

Look for these symptoms: a coordinator that does all the work itself (missing Task tool), a synthesis that ignores earlier findings (findings not passed), lost citations (metadata not structured), slow runs (Task calls spread across turns), or rigid subagents (procedural prompts). Claims that subagents "automatically share memory" or "inherit the parent's history" are wrong.

Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns. When a step must happen before another, enforce it in code rather than asking nicely in the prompt; split multi-issue requests into items; and hand off to humans with a structured summary they can act on.
What you need to know

There are two ways to make an agent do steps in order: Prompt-based guidance Programmatic enforcement How "Always verify the customer before looking up orders" in the system prompt Code that blocks the downstream tool until the prerequisite has succeeded Reliability High, but not 100% : a persuasive message or an unusual case can skip it Deterministic: the blocked call cannot run Good for Preferences, tone, ordering that is nice to have Rules with legal, financial or security consequences When a requirement is deterministic , such as "identity must be verified before any financial operation", a prompt alone has a non-zero failure rate. In production, a 1% failure rate across 50,000 contacts is 500 refunds to unverified callers. The exam expects you to recognise this and choose enforcement in code.

A prerequisite gate tracks what has happened in the session and refuses calls that come too early. verified = {} # session_id -> customer_id, set when get_customer verifies def gate(session_id, tool_name): if tool_name in ("lookup_order", "process_refund") and session_id not in verified: return "Blocked: verify the customer with get_customer first." return None # allowed In the Agent SDK this check usually lives in a PreToolUse hook (lesson 1.5), which denies the call and tells Claude why, so Claude can go back and verify.

Customers often raise several problems in one message: a damaged item, a wrong address and missing loyalty points. Handling only the first one and asking "anything else?" damages first-contact resolution. The stronger pattern: 1. Decompose the message into distinct items. 2. Investigate each against the shared customer context (one verification, one customer record), in parallel where the items are independent. 3. Synthesise one reply that resolves or explains each item.

docs.c: Guaranteed means code · Louder prompts · Escalating because there are several issues
docs.x: When the agent escalates mid-process, the human agent usually cannot see the transcript . A handoff that says "customer has a billing issue, please help" forces the human to start again and the customer to repeat themselves. A structured handoff carries what the human needs to act: Field Example Customer ID and verification status C-118204, verified by email and order number The issue, in one line Charged twice for order 55107 Root cause found so far Payment retried after a gateway timeout Amounts and references $219.90, orders 55107 and 55107-R Actions already taken Refund of the duplicate requested, rejected: over limit Recommended next action Approve the $219.90 refund of the duplicate charge If the business says "must always" or "must never", enforce it with a gate or hook. Use the prompt to explain the rule to Claude, not to guarantee it. Options that move the rule to the top of the prompt, put it in capitals, repeat it, or add "CRITICAL" improve the odds a little. They do not remove the failure rate the scenario has already measured. A message with three concerns is not a reason to escalate. Decompose and resolve; escalate only the items that meet an escalation trigger.

Scenario 1 (customer support) carries most of these. Typical stems: a measured rate of skipped verification, refunds that bypass a rule, a multi-part message handled partially, or human agents complaining that escalations are useless. Choose code-level enforcement for hard rules, decomposition for multi-concern messages, and a structured summary for handoffs.

docs.t: Agent SDK Hooks: Interception and Normalization
docs.x: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization. Hooks run your code at fixed points in the agent loop. PreToolUse hooks block or redirect tool calls before they run; PostToolUse hooks reshape tool results before Claude sees them. Use them when a rule must hold every time.

docs.t: Agent SDK Hooks: Interception and Normalization
docs.x: A hook is a callback the agent runtime calls at a fixed point in the loop. Two hook events matter most for this task: Event Fires Typical use PreToolUse After Claude requests a tool, before it runs Block policy-violating calls, redirect to another workflow, rewrite inputs PostToolUse After the tool runs, before Claude sees the result Normalise formats, trim fields, add context Hooks attach to tools through a matcher on the tool name. MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool> , so a hook for Cedar Ridge's refund tool matches mcp__support__process_refund .

docs.t: Agent SDK Hooks: Interception and Normalization
docs.x: A PreToolUse hook inspects the call and returns a decision. To block, it returns deny with a reason. The reason goes back to Claude, which can then take the alternative path, such as escalating. async def refund_limit(input_data, tool_use_id, context): amount = input_data["tool_input"].get("amount", 0) if amount > 500: return {"hookSpecificOutput": { "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny", "permissionDecisionReason": "Refunds over $500 need a human. Call escalate_to_human with a summary."}} return {} # allow options = ClaudeAgentOptions(hooks={"PreToolUse": [ HookMatcher(matcher="mcp__support__process_refund", hooks=[refund_limit])]})

docs.t: Agent SDK Hooks: Interception and Normalization
docs.x: Different tools return the same kind of data in different shapes: Unix epoch seconds from one, ISO 8601 strings from another, numeric status codes from a third. Left alone, Claude has to reconcile them in every turn and sometimes gets it wrong. A PostToolUse hook converts everything to one format before the model reasons about it. Current SDKs let the hook replace the result (the updatedToolOutput field) or append a note ( additionalContext ). STATUS = {0: "succeeded", 2: "pending", 5: "rejected"} def normalise(result: dict) -> dict: out = dict(result) if "created" in out and isinstance(out["created"], int): out["created"] = datetime.fromtimestamp(out["created"], tz=timezone.utc).isoformat() if "status" in out and isinstance(out["status"], int): out["status"] = STATUS.get(out["status"], "unknown") return out The same normalisation could live inside each tool. A hook is the right place when you do not own the tools, or when you want one rule applied to all of them.

docs.t: Agent SDK Hooks: Interception and Normalization
docs.c: Hook for "must", prompt for "should" · The tool description as a guardrail · Temperature as a compliance setting · Claude Code uses the same idea
docs.x: This is the idea the exam tests hardest. A rule written in the system prompt is followed with high probability . A rule enforced by a hook is followed every time , because the call never reaches the tool. When a business rule requires guaranteed compliance (refund limits, blocked file paths, approval before changes), choose the hook. Use hooks for rules whose breach has a real cost. Use the prompt for guidance, tone and preferences, and to explain to Claude what the hooks will enforce. Writing "CRITICAL: never exceed $500" in the tool description is still prompt-level guidance. It reduces violations; it does not prevent them. Setting temperature to 0 makes output more repeatable. It does not turn a probabilistic rule into a guaranteed one. In Claude Code, a PostToolUse hook on Write and Edit can run the formatter and linter after every file change, whether or not the instructions mention formatting. A PreToolUse hook can block writes to protected paths. The pattern is identical: deterministic code at a fixed point in the loop.

Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows. Use a fixed chain of steps when the work is predictable and an adaptive plan when each finding changes what to do next; split large reviews into per-file passes plus an integration pass.

Decomposition is how a large task becomes a set of smaller ones. The exam asks you to choose between two families. Fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining) Dynamic, adaptive decomposition Shape The same steps in the same order every time The next subtask is chosen from what the last one found Fits Predictable, multi-aspect work: a review that always checks the same five things Open-ended investigation: an incident, an unknown codebase Strength Cheap, testable, easy to debug Handles what nobody anticipated Weakness Cannot react to surprises Harder to predict cost and time

A chain passes each step's output into the next. A code review chain might be: analyse each file on its own, then run one cross-file pass that checks how the files fit together. Each prompt is small and focused, and you can add a gate between steps: for example, if linting finds severe problems, skip type checks and go straight to the summary.

A single prompt asked to review 20 files at once suffers attention dilution : some files get careful attention, others a skim, and findings can contradict each other. The fix is two kinds of pass: 1. Per-file local passes , one file at a time, for local issues. 2. A separate integration pass for cross-file concerns: data flow, interface mismatches, duplicated logic.

docs.c: Predictable work gets a chain; uncertain work gets a plan that adapts · Starting with the easiest subtask · One giant review prompt · Two workflows, two choices
docs.x: Some tasks cannot be planned up front. "Add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase" with no further detail is an example. A good decomposition does not start writing tests; it: 1. Maps the structure : modules, entry points, dependencies, existing coverage. 2. Identifies high-impact areas : code that changes often, handles money, or has no tests. 3. Creates a prioritised plan , then adapts it as dependencies and surprises are discovered. Ask whether you could write the steps down before seeing any data. If yes, chain them. If no, decompose adaptively. For open-ended work, options that start testing the simplest module "to build momentum" skip the mapping step. The exam rewards understanding the structure first. Feeding every changed file into one prompt "so the model sees the whole picture" causes dilution. The whole picture belongs in a dedicated integration pass. A weekly review that always checks security, error handling, naming, tests and documentation is a five-step chain. A production incident where each log line suggests the next place to look needs dynamic decomposition: each finding generates the next subtask.

docs.x: Manage session state, resumption, and forking. Resume a named session when its context is still true, fork it to try two approaches from the same analysis, and start fresh with a summary when the code has moved on and old tool results are stale.

docs.t: Sessions: Resume, Fork or Start Fresh
docs.x: A session is the conversation history the agent has built: your prompts, every tool call, every tool result, every response. Returning to it means the agent has all of that again, including the files it already read and the conclusions it already reached. The exam tests three ways to go back, and when each one is right. Approach What it does Use it when Resume Continues an existing session, adding to its history The earlier context is still mostly valid Fork Copies the history into a new, independent session; the original is untouched You want to try two or more directions from the same starting analysis Start fresh with a summary A new session whose first message carries a structured summary of earlier conclusions The earlier tool results no longer describe the code

docs.x: In Claude Code you can name a session and come back to it the next day with --resume : claude --resume leak-hunt In the Agent SDK you capture the session ID from the result message and pass it to the resume option. Either way, the agent continues with full context.

docs.x: After a long analysis of a module, you might want to compare two refactoring strategies. Running both in one session muddles them; repeating the analysis twice wastes the work. A fork branches the conversation: options = ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=analysis_session_id, fork_session=True) Each fork gets its own session ID and diverges independently. Note that a fork branches the conversation , not the files: if both forks edit the same working directory, they edit the same files.

docs.t: Sessions: Resume, Fork or Start Fresh

docs.x: A resumed session trusts its old tool results. If teammates have since changed 15 of the 20 files the session read, those results describe code that no longer exists, and the agent will reason confidently from them. Two remedies: - If a few files changed, resume and tell the agent exactly which files changed so it re-reads only those. That is targeted re-analysis, not full re-exploration. - If most of the context is stale, start a new session seeded with a structured summary: the conclusions, decisions and open questions from the old one, without its out-of-date tool results. Mostly true: resume (and name what changed). Mostly stale: start fresh with a summary. Need two directions from one baseline: fork. "Resume, because it keeps all the context" sounds efficient. Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries. Claude chooses tools by reading their descriptions, so a description must say what the tool does, what it accepts, what it returns and when to use it instead of its neighbours.

When Claude decides which tool to call, the description is the main thing it has to go on. The name helps, the schema helps, but the description carries the meaning. A one-line description ("Retrieves customer information") is the commonest reason an agent picks the wrong tool among similar ones.

Element Example for lookup_order What it does Returns one order's items, status, dates and payment Inputs and their format order_id : the order number, 5 to 7 digits, with or without a leading # What it returns Order status, item list, delivery date, refund eligibility When to use it When the customer gives an order number or asks about a specific delivery When not to use it To find a customer by name or email: use get_customer Edge cases Returns found: false for an unknown number; that is not an error {"name": "lookup_order", "description": "Look up one order by its order number (5-7 digits, '#' optional). Returns status, items, delivery date and refund eligibility. Use when the customer names an order or a specific delivery. Do not use to find a customer: use get_customer with an email, phone or account number. An unknown number returns found=false, which is a valid result.", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^#?[0-9]{5,7}$"}}, "required": ["order_id"]}}

Two tools with near-identical descriptions, such as analyze_content and analyze_document , force Claude to guess. The fixes are to rename and re-describe so each tool's purpose is distinct (for example, analyze_content becomes extract_web_results , described as working only on fetched web pages), or to split a generic tool.

docs.h: Split generic tools into purpose-specific ones
docs.x: A single analyze_document tool with a mode parameter for extraction, summarisation and claim verification asks Claude to pick the tool and the mode, and it often gets the mode wrong. Three tools with their own input and output contracts are easier to choose between: - extract_data_points(document_id, fields) returns structured values - summarize_content(document_id, length) returns a summary - verify_claim_against_source(claim, document_id) returns supported, contradicted or not found, with the passage Constrained inputs help too. A free-text language parameter collects "python", "Python3" and "py"; an enum of allowed values does not.

docs.h: The system prompt can override good descriptions
docs.c: Describe the boundary, not just the purpose · More examples in the system prompt · Merging tools to "simplify"
docs.x: Tool selection is also shaped by the system prompt. An instruction like "always search before answering" can create an unintended association with any tool whose name contains "search", even when another tool fits better. When tools are misrouted despite good descriptions, review the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions. Every description should say when to use the tool and when to use something else. The boundary sentence is what stops misrouting. When two tools are confused, adding routing examples to the system prompt treats the symptom. The exam prefers fixing the tool descriptions, names or split, because that is where selection happens. Combining similar tools into one with a mode flag looks tidy but moves the confusion into a parameter. Purpose-specific tools are the stronger answer.

Expect logs showing two tools confused, a generic tool used in the wrong mode, or a capable tool ignored. Choose answers that rewrite descriptions with inputs, outputs and boundaries, rename to remove overlap, split generic tools, or constrain inputs with enums.

Implement structured error responses for MCP tools. A tool failure should come back flagged as an error, with a category, a retryable flag and a plain description, so the agent can choose between retrying, asking the user, explaining a policy or escalating.
What you need to know

An MCP tool reports a failure by returning its result with isError: true . If a tool instead returns "Error: could not parse document" as an ordinary, successful text result, the agent may treat the error message as the document's content and reason from it. The flag tells the agent "this call failed", not "this is what the document says".

docs.h: Not all errors are the same
docs.x: Category Example Right response Transient Timeout, service unavailable Retry, perhaps after a short wait Validation Order number in the wrong format Fix the input or ask the user; retrying unchanged will fail again Business Refund outside the 45-day window Do not retry; explain the policy to the customer Permission Agent not allowed to see payroll data Do not retry; escalate or explain A uniform "Operation failed" hides all of this. The agent cannot tell a timeout (retry) from a policy rejection (explain), so it either retries things that will never succeed or gives up on things that would.

{"isError": true, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "{\"errorCategory\": \"business\", \"isRetryable\": false, \"message\": \"Order 55107 was delivered 61 days ago; returns close after 45 days.\", \"customerMessage\": \"This order is outside our 45-day return window.\"}"}]} - errorCategory lets the agent pick a recovery strategy. - isRetryable prevents wasted retries. - A human-readable message explains what happened; for business errors, a customer-friendly explanation lets the agent tell the customer something accurate.

docs.h: Recover locally, propagate what you cannot fix
docs.x: In a multi-agent system, a subagent should retry transient failures itself . Only errors it cannot resolve go up to the coordinator, together with what was attempted and any partial results . The coordinator then decides: try another source, re-scope the task, or report a gap.

docs.c: Category plus retryable · Returning errors as successful results · Retry everything
docs.x: A search that runs successfully and finds nothing is a valid empty result : "no orders for this customer". A search that could not run is an access failure . Reporting the first as an error triggers pointless retries; reporting the second as an empty success silently hides a gap. Keep them distinct. Every error a tool returns should say what kind of error it is and whether retrying could help. If the scenario says the agent "treats the error message as content", the fix is the isError flag, not a better prompt. Automatic retries for all failures waste calls on validation, business and permission errors that will fail the same way every time.

Look for "Operation failed" everywhere, an agent retrying policy rejections, an error parsed as content, or a subagent that returns "no results" when the search actually timed out. Pick structured categories, the isError flag, local retry for transient failures, and a clear split between failure and empty.

Distribute tools appropriately across agents and configure tool choice. Give each agent only the tools its role needs, replace open-ended tools with constrained ones, and use tool_choice to force a tool, require some tool, or leave the choice to Claude.
What you need to know

Every tool an agent can see is another option to weigh on every turn. An agent with 18 tools chooses less reliably than one with 4 or 5 , and an agent holding tools outside its specialty will use them: a synthesis agent with a web search tool starts searching instead of synthesising. Scoped tool access gives each agent the tools its role needs, set in its AgentDefinition tools list. Subagent Tools Web search web_search , fetch_page Document analysis read_document , extract_tables Synthesis verify_fact (one narrow cross-role tool)

Sometimes a role genuinely needs a little of another role's ability. The synthesis agent may need to check a date or a figure many times per report; sending each check back through the coordinator is slow. Give it a scoped tool such as verify_fact for simple lookups, and keep complex research routed through the coordinator.

A fetch_url tool that accepts any URL gets used for API endpoints, binary files and internal admin pages. Replace it with a constrained alternative, such as load_document , that validates the URL against an approved pattern before fetching. The constraint lives in the tool, so it holds regardless of what the model tries.

docs.c: Tools follow the role · "Give everyone everything, so no one is blocked" · auto when output must be structured
docs.x: Setting Effect Use when {"type": "auto"} Claude may call a tool or reply in text The default for conversational agents {"type": "any"} Claude must call a tool, but chooses which You need structured output and there are several possible schemas {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} Claude must call that tool A specific step must run first Forced selection applies to one request. A common pattern is to force extract_metadata on the first call, then process its result and let later steps (such as enrichment) run in follow-up turns with auto or any . first = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, tools=TOOLS, tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": doc}]) Start every agent with the smallest tool set that does its job. Add a cross-role tool only for a specific, frequent need. Full catalogues for every subagent look flexible. They degrade selection and invite misuse, which is the failure the scenario usually describes. With auto , Claude may answer in prose. If the stem says every response must be a structured extraction, any (or a forced tool) is the fix.

Expect a system where every agent has every tool, an agent misusing a tool from another role, a broad tool being abused, or a step that must run first. Map: role-scoped tools, a narrow cross-role tool, a constrained replacement, any to guarantee a tool call, a forced tool to guarantee order.

What you need to know

docs.h: Where a server is configured decides who gets it
docs.x: Scope File Shared? Use for Project .mcp.json in the repository Yes, through version control Team tooling: the issue tracker, the shared GitHub server User ~/.claude.json No, only you Personal or experimental servers A server in the project file reaches every teammate and every CI runner on clone, with no per-machine setup to drift. An experimental server in the project file reaches everyone too, which is usually not what you want.

docs.h: Keep secrets out of the repository
docs.x: Project configuration is committed, so it must not contain tokens. .mcp.json supports environment variable expansion : {"mcpServers": { "github": { "command": "github-mcp-server", "env": {"GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"} }}} Each developer (and the CI system) sets GITHUB_TOKEN in their own environment.

docs.h: All servers' tools are available at once
docs.x: Tools from every configured MCP server are discovered when the agent connects and are available together , alongside the built-in tools. That is convenient, and it is also why tool count and description quality (lessons 2.1 and 2.3) matter.

docs.h: Make MCP tools win when they should
docs.x: An agent often prefers a built-in like Grep over a more capable MCP tool, such as a semantic code search, because the MCP tool's description does not explain what it can do. The fix is a richer description of capabilities and outputs, and of when to prefer it over Grep.
For standard integrations (Jira, GitHub, common databases), prefer an existing community MCP server over writing your own. Reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows nobody else has built.

docs.c: Shared in the project, personal in the user file, secrets in the environment · Committing the token · Disabling the built-in tool

An MCP resource exposes such a catalogue (a documentation hierarchy, a database schema, a list of issue summaries) as content the agent can read directly, so it knows what is available without exploratory tool calls. That one sentence answers most MCP configuration questions. Any option that puts a literal token in .mcp.json is wrong, however convenient. Use ${VAR} expansion. Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) effectively. Grep searches file contents, Glob matches file paths, Read and Write handle whole files and Edit makes targeted changes; build understanding incrementally instead of reading everything up front.
What you need to know

Tool Searches or changes Example Grep File contents , by pattern Every caller of calculateTax ; every place that throws RateLimitExceeded Glob File paths , by name pattern Every test file: / .test.tsx Read One whole file Load a file to understand or change it Write One whole file Create a file, or replace one entirely Edit Part of a file, by unique text match Change one line in a 2,000-line file Bash Commands Run tests, a build, git The distinction the exam tests most is Grep versus Glob : contents versus names. Finding files called .test.tsx is Glob; finding files that contain "PaymentDeclinedError" is Grep.

Edit replaces a piece of text that must appear exactly once in the file. For a small change in a large file it is preferred over rewriting the whole file, because nothing else can be lost or altered by accident. If the anchor text is not unique (the same boilerplate appears six times), Edit fails. Two good responses: - Include more surrounding text so the match becomes unique. - Fall back to Read the whole file, make the change in the full text, and Write it back.

Asked "how does billing work?", an agent that reads all 30 files in the directory fills its context before it has answered anything. The better approach: 1. Grep for entry points: exported functions, main classes, route handlers. 2. Read those files. 3. Follow imports and calls with further Reads, only along the paths that matter.

docs.c: Contents with Grep, names with Glob, small changes with Edit · Read everything first · Bash for everything
docs.x: When a function is re-exported through wrapper modules (sometimes under a different name), a single Grep for its original name misses callers. First find every name it is exported under , then Grep for each name. Grep "calculate_tax" in pricing/ -> defined in pricing/tax.py Grep "from pricing.tax import" -> re-exported as compute_tax in billing/__init__.py Grep "compute_tax calculate_tax" in src -> all real call sites Then: Read plus Write when Edit cannot find a unique anchor. "Read all the files so nothing is missed" sounds thorough and exhausts context. Grep first, then read selectively. Running find and grep through Bash works, but when a dedicated tool fits, the exam prefers it.

Scenario 4 (developer productivity) is the home of these questions: a pair of search tasks to match to Grep and Glob, a failing Edit, an agent drowning in file reads, or callers missed through wrappers.

Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization. CLAUDE.md files load from user, project and directory levels; only the project level is shared through version control. Keep them modular with @import and .claude/rules/, and check what loaded with /memory.
What you need to know

Level Location Applies to Shared with the team? User ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md You, in every project No Project CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md at the repository root Everyone working in the repository Yes, through version control Directory CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory Work in that part of the tree Yes, if committed The classic failure: a new teammate's sessions ignore the team's standards, because the standards were written in a senior engineer's user-level file. That file never left the senior engineer's machine. The fix is to move the standards into the project CLAUDE.md.
The /memory command shows which memory files the current session has loaded. When behaviour differs between people or sessions, it is the first thing to check.

A single CLAUDE.md that grows to 2,000 lines is loaded in full every session, whatever the task. Two tools keep it manageable: - @import pulls another file into a CLAUDE.md. A package's CLAUDE.md can import only the standards that package needs: # api/CLAUDE.md @../docs/standards/typescript.md @../docs/standards/error-handling.md API handlers use async/await and the typed errors in src/errors. - .claude/rules/ holds topic files ( testing.md , api-conventions.md , deployment.md ) as an alternative to one monolithic file. Rules can also be scoped to paths so they load only when relevant (lesson 3.3).

A zero-tolerance security rule needs a hook or a permission deny rule. If the team needs it, commit it in the project's CLAUDE.md or rules. The user file is for you alone. Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading. Rule files in .claude/rules/ can carry a paths glob in their frontmatter so they load only when Claude works on matching files, which suits conventions that follow file types across the whole tree.

A rule file in .claude/rules/ can declare which files it applies to, using glob patterns in YAML frontmatter. The rule loads only when Claude is working on a matching file. paths: [" / .test.tsx", " / .test.ts", " / .spec. "] # Testing conventions - Use the fixtures in test/fixtures; never build test data inline. - One behaviour per test; name tests "does X when Y". - Use React Testing Library queries by role, not by class name. paths: ["infra/ / .tf"] # Terraform conventions - Modules only; no inline resources. - Every resource carries the owner and cost-centre tags.

- Less irrelevant context. Terraform rules do not load while someone edits React components. - Fewer tokens in every session that does not touch those files. - Conventions that follow file type, not folder. Test files sit next to the code they test, all over the tree. A directory-level CLAUDE.md cannot reach them all without being copied into every folder; one glob, / .test.tsx , does.

Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution. Plan mode lets Claude explore and design before changing anything; use it for large, multi-file or architectural work and go straight to execution for small, clear changes. Use the Explore subagent to keep noisy discovery out of the main context.
What you need to know

In plan mode Claude reads and explores but does not edit files or run changing commands. It produces a plan for you to review. That makes it safe to investigate a codebase and agree on a design before any change is made, which prevents expensive rework.

Use plan mode for Use direct execution for Large-scale changes across many files A single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace Several valid approaches to choose between Adding one validation check to one function Architectural decisions (service boundaries, API contracts) A well-understood change with a clear scope Library or framework migrations (45+ files) Renaming a local variable Integrations with different infrastructure needs Fixing a typo in a comment The test is uncertainty and blast radius . If you could describe the exact change in a sentence and it touches one place, execute. If the right approach is not yet clear, or a wrong start would mean undoing dozens of files, plan first.
The modes combine. A library migration is planned (explore usages, choose a strategy, agree the order) and then executed directly, following the agreed plan.

docs.c: Unclear or wide: plan. Clear and narrow: execute. · "Direct execution is faster" · Planning everything
docs.x: Discovery is noisy: Grep results, file listings, dependency traces. In a multi-phase task, that output can fill the main context before implementation starts. The built-in Explore subagent does the discovery in its own context and returns a summary , so the main conversation reaches the implementation phase with room to work. And when discovery will be verbose, delegate it to Explore. For a microservice split or a 50-file migration, starting to edit immediately is the slow path once rework is counted. The exam rewards planning these. Plan mode for a one-line fix with a known cause adds ceremony and no value.

Many questions present two tasks side by side (a small fix and a large migration) and ask for the right mode for each. Others describe context running out during a long discovery phase, which points to the Explore subagent.

Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement. When prose instructions are read inconsistently, show concrete input and output examples, drive the work with tests, let Claude interview you before building in unfamiliar territory, and batch interacting issues into one message.
Getting the result you want from Claude Code is usually a short series of refinements. The exam tests four techniques and when each fits.

When a prose description ("normalise the phone numbers") produces inconsistent results, two or three concrete examples remove the ambiguity faster than more prose: Input: "(020) 7946 0958" -> Output: "+442079460958" Input: "07700 900123" -> Output: "+447700900123" Input: "+44 20 7946 0958" -> Output: "+442079460958" The same applies to edge cases: to fix crashes on null values in a migration script, give specific test cases with sample input containing nulls and the expected output.

Write the test suite first: expected behaviour, edge cases, and any performance requirement. Then let Claude implement, run the tests, and share the failures to guide the next round. Tests give Claude an objective way to verify its own work, so each iteration converges instead of drifting.

In an unfamiliar domain you may not know what you do not know. Ask Claude to interview you before writing code: it asks about the considerations you might miss (cache invalidation, failure modes, consistency, retention), and the answers become the specification.

docs.c: Show, test, ask, then group · More adjectives · Fixing interacting bugs one by one
docs.x: Issues Approach Interacting : a race condition causes a null pointer, which produces a misleading error message One detailed message describing all of them, because fixing one changes the others Independent : a typo in a config file and an unrelated slow query Fix them one at a time, so each change is small and easy to verify Examples for ambiguous transformations; tests for verifiable behaviour; interviews for unfamiliar domains; one message for interacting problems. "Be more careful with the formatting" or "make it robust" does not reduce inconsistency. Concrete examples and tests do. Sequential fixes for coupled bugs lead to churn: each fix is undone or invalidated by the next.

Stems describe an inconsistent transformation (examples), an edge case to fix (test cases with input and output), an unfamiliar feature (interview), or several bugs at once (decide whether they interact).

Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines. In CI, run Claude Code non-interactively with -p, get machine-readable findings with --output-format json and --json-schema, give it project context through CLAUDE.md, and review with a separate instance from the one that wrote the code.
What you need to know

A CI job has no one to answer prompts. Run Claude Code with -p ( --print ): it processes the prompt, prints the result and exits. Without it, the job waits for terminal input until the pipeline times out. claude -p "Review this pull request for security issues" \

- --output-format json returns machine-readable output instead of prose. - --json-schema makes the final output match a schema you supply. Together they produce findings a script can post as inline PR comments without fragile text parsing: {"findings": [{"file": "src/pay.ts", "line": 88, "severity": "high", "category": "security", "issue": "Card number logged in plain text", "fix": "Log only the last four digits"}]}

CI-invoked Claude Code reads the project's CLAUDE.md . That is where to document testing standards, the fixture library, what makes a valuable test, and the review criteria. Generated tests that ignore fixtures or test trivial getters usually mean this context is missing.

- When a review re-runs after new commits , include the previous findings in context and ask Claude to report only new issues or earlier ones still unaddressed. Otherwise it re-posts everything, and developers mute it. - When generating tests, include the existing test files so Claude does not suggest scenarios already covered.

Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives. Precision comes from saying exactly what to report and what to skip, with severity defined by concrete examples, not from asking Claude to be conservative. Noisy categories can be switched off while they are fixed.
What you need to know

docs.h: Vague instructions do not move precision
docs.x: "Be conservative", "only report high-confidence findings" and "be very, very careful" sound like they should cut false positives. In practice they change little, because they do not tell Claude what counts . Precision improves when the prompt defines the categories to report and the ones to skip. Vague Explicit "Check that comments are accurate" "Flag a comment only when the behaviour it claims contradicts what the code does" "Only report important issues" "Report: bugs that change behaviour, security issues, data loss. Skip: style, naming, patterns used consistently elsewhere in this repository" "Be conservative" "If the issue depends on an assumption you cannot verify from the diff, do not report it"

docs.h: False positives destroy trust in everything
docs.x: Developers do not judge categories separately. If the style category is wrong 70% of the time, they start dismissing all findings, including accurate security ones. A high false-positive category damages the categories that work. A practical response: temporarily disable the noisy category so developers trust the rest again, and improve its prompt offline before re-enabling it.

docs.c: Categories, not confidence · Adding intensity · Leaving the noisy category on while tuning
docs.x: "Critical" and "minor" drift unless each level is defined with criteria and a concrete code example : Severity Criteria Example Critical Exploitable security flaw or data loss in production SQL built by string concatenation from request input High Wrong behaviour users will hit Refund calculated before discount is applied Medium Wrong behaviour in rare paths Missing null check on an optional field Low Maintainability Duplicated helper that already exists in utils Tell Claude which issues to report and which to skip, and define each severity with an example. "Be very, very conservative" and "only report if you are certain" are the distractors. They have no measurable effect in the scenarios the exam describes. Every day it stays on, trust in the accurate categories keeps falling.

Scenario 5 again: a reviewer with a high false-positive rate, developers ignoring all findings, or inconsistent severity labels. The answer defines report and skip categories, uses examples for severity, or disables a noisy category temporarily.

Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality. When instructions alone give inconsistent results, two to four well-chosen examples fix the format and teach judgement on ambiguous cases. Choose examples that show reasoning, cover the hard cases, and match the work being done.
What you need to know

Detailed instructions describe what you want; examples show it . When instructions produce inconsistent formats or judgement, few-shot examples are the most effective fix. They do three jobs: - Fix the output format : every finding has location, issue, severity and suggested fix, in the same order. - Show judgement on ambiguous cases : which tool to use for an unclear request; whether an uncovered branch matters. - Help Claude generalise : from a few well-reasoned examples it handles new patterns, not only the ones listed.

Two to four targeted examples usually beat twenty. Spend them on the ambiguous cases, not the obvious ones, and include the reasoning : why this action was chosen over a plausible alternative. <example> Code: switch (s) { case A: start(); / falls through / case B: run(); } Decision: skip Reason: the comment marks the fall-through as intentional. </example> <example> Code: switch (s) { case A: start(); case B: run(); } Decision: report (medium) Reason: no break and no comment; likely an accidental fall-through. </example> Pairs like these, an acceptable pattern next to a genuine issue , cut false positives while still catching real bugs.

Examples also reduce hallucination and empty fields in extraction: - Show correct extraction from varied structures : inline citations versus a bibliography; a methodology section versus details scattered in the text. - Show informal values handled correctly ("about two metres" becomes {"value": 2, "unit": "m", "approximate": true} ). - Show date formats from several sources all normalised to one output format.

docs.c: Few, hard, reasoned · Twenty examples to cover everything · Examples that do not match the input
docs.x: Examples are powerful in both directions. If all your examples are short Python functions, results on a 200-line Go file will lean towards short Python habits. Choose examples that match the kind of input the prompt will see, or vary them deliberately. Two to four examples aimed at the ambiguous cases, each with a reason and the exact output format. A long list of easy cases costs context and still misses the hard ones. Fewer, harder examples generalise better. Examples from a different language, size or document type bias the output towards the wrong patterns.

Look for inconsistent formatting despite detailed instructions, intentional patterns flagged as bugs, wrong tool choice on ambiguous requests, empty required fields in extraction, or weak results on inputs unlike the examples.

docs.h: Tool use as the output channel
docs.x: "Respond with JSON" in a prompt usually works, and occasionally returns markdown fences, a trailing comma or a sentence of prose. The reliable approach: define an extraction tool whose input_schema is the JSON schema you want, have Claude call it, and read the structured data from the tool_use block . With strict tool use, the arguments match the schema, which removes JSON syntax errors. extract_invoice = { "name": "extract_invoice", "description": "Record the fields of one invoice.", "strict": True, # strict tool use: arguments follow the schema "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "vendor_name": {"type": "string"}, "vendor_tax_id": {"type": ["string", "null"]}, "invoice_date": {"type": "string", "description": "YYYY-MM-DD"}, "category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["goods", "services", "utilities", "other"]}, "category_detail": {"type": ["string", "null"]}, "total": {"type": "number"}}, "required": ["vendor_name", "vendor_tax_id", "invoice_date", "category", "total"]}} resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, tools=[extract_invoice], tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}, messages=msgs) data = next(b.input for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use")

docs.h: Design the schema so the model never has to invent
docs.x: - Nullable or optional fields for information a document may not contain. A required vendor_tax_id with no tax ID in the document pushes the model to fabricate one; "type": ["string", "null"] lets it say "not present". - Enums with an escape hatch : "other" plus a category_detail string for documents that fit no category, and "unclear" for genuinely ambiguous cases. - Normalisation rules in the prompt ("dates as YYYY-MM-DD; amounts as numbers without currency symbols") alongside the schema, because sources are inconsistent.

docs.c: Tool for structure, nullable for absence, validation for truth · Required fields for everything · "The schema guarantees accuracy"
docs.x: A schema guarantees the output parses and has the right types . It does not guarantee the values are right : line items that do not sum to the total, a vendor name in the address field, a date from the wrong part of the page. Those are semantic errors, and they need validation (lesson 4.4). Tool use removes syntax errors; schema design removes forced fabrication; semantic checks catch the rest. Making every field required "for completeness" is how fabricated values appear. Required means the model must produce something. Valid JSON can still be wrong. Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality. Validate extractions for meaning, not just shape; retry with the document, the failed output and the exact errors; know that retries cannot recover information the document does not contain; and record patterns so dismissals can be analysed.
What you need to know

Syntax / schema errors Semantic errors Example Missing bracket, wrong type Line items do not sum to the total; vendor name in the address field Removed by Tool use with a strict schema Validation code that checks meaning

Ask the model to extract values that make errors visible : - calculated_total (the sum of line items) alongside stated_total , so a mismatch is flagged instead of hidden. - conflict_detected: true when the document contradicts itself, such as two different totals. Validation code then compares fields and decides whether to accept, retry or route to a person.

A blind retry ("try again") often repeats the same mistake. An effective retry sends: 1. The original document . 2. The failed extraction . 3. The specific validation errors : " invoice_date is 'next Tuesday'; expected YYYY-MM-DD. total is 'approximately $500'; expected a number." for attempt in range(2): data = extract(document, feedback) errors = validate(data) # semantic and format checks if not errors: break feedback = {"previous": data, "errors": errors}

Retries fix format mismatches and structural mistakes. They cannot produce information the document does not contain . If the purchase order number appears only in a separate document that was not provided, three more retries will either fail or invent one. Detect this case and route it elsewhere: return null, request the other document, or send it to review.

Design efficient batch processing strategies. The Message Batches API halves the cost of work that can wait up to 24 hours, with no latency guarantee. Use it for overnight and backlog jobs, never for blocking checks, correlate results by custom_id, and resubmit only what failed.
What you need to know

Synchronous Messages API Message Batches API Cost Standard About 50% less When you get results Seconds Within 24 hours ; often much sooner, but no latency SLA Tool calls mid-request Yes, your loop runs tools between calls No : a batch request cannot pause to run a tool and continue

docs.h: Match the API to the workflow
docs.x: - Batch : overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation, a backlog of historical documents due tomorrow. Nobody is waiting. - Synchronous : anything that blocks a person or a process, such as a pre-merge check developers wait on, or a live chat.

Each request in a batch carries a custom_id you choose (for example the document ID). Results are matched back to inputs by that ID, not by position. requests = [{"custom_id": doc.id, "params": {"model": MODEL, "max_tokens": 1024, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": doc.text}]}} for doc in docs] batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=requests)

When 200 of 10,000 requests fail, identify them by custom_id , fix the cause, and resubmit only those . Fixes depend on the failure: chunk documents that exceeded the context limit; simply resubmit transient errors. Reprocessing all 10,000 doubles the cost for no gain.

Then correlate by custom_id and resubmit only the failures. "Use batches for the pre-merge check to halve the cost" ignores the missing latency guarantee. A check that may take hours cannot block a merge. A batch request cannot run your tools and continue in the same request. Multi-turn tool workflows need the synchronous loop.

Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures. A model reviewing its own work in the same session tends to approve it, so review with an independent instance. Split large reviews into per-file passes plus an integration pass, and have findings carry confidence for routing.
What you need to know

A session that generated code still holds the reasoning that led to it. Asked to review, it tends to agree with itself : the same assumptions that produced a bug make the bug look correct. Adding "review critically" or turning on extended thinking in the same session helps less than you would hope. An independent instance , a fresh session that sees the code but not the generator's reasoning, catches more subtle issues. Design Catches subtle issues? Same session, "now review your code" Rarely Same session with more thinking Somewhat Independent instance with the diff and the standards Best of the three

A single pass over a 25-file change spreads attention thin: some files get skimmed, and findings can contradict each other. Split the work: 1. Per-file local passes : one file at a time, for local bugs, error handling and security issues. 2. Integration pass : across files, for data flow, interface mismatches and assumptions one file makes about another.

More reasoning in the same context still carries the generator's assumptions. Independence is the fix the exam wants.

Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions. Summaries lose numbers, dates and promises, long inputs lose their middles, and verbose tool results crowd out what matters. Keep transactional facts in a persistent block, trim tool output, and put key findings first.
What you need to know

docs.h: Three ways long interactions lose information
docs.x: 1. Progressive summarisation. To save space, older turns are summarised. Summaries turn "$127.43 refund for order #889234, return window ends 14 March" into "the customer discussed a refund". Numbers, percentages, dates and what the customer was promised are exactly what gets lost. 2. Lost in the middle. Models use the beginning and end of a long input reliably, and may under-use material in the middle. In an aggregated input of six subagents' findings, the third and fourth are most at risk. 3. Tool result bloat. Every tool result stays in the conversation. An order lookup returning 40 fields, of which 5 matter for a return, spends tokens on 35 irrelevant ones every turn after. Also remember the basics: the API is stateless, so each request must carry the complete conversation history you want Claude to use. Dropping turns silently breaks coherence.

Keep transactional facts outside the summarised history, in a structured block included in every prompt: <case_facts> customer: C-118204 (verified) issue_1: order 55107, tent torn, refund $219.90 approved, status: processing issue_2: order 54980, 340 loyalty points missing, status: credited promised: refund confirmation email within 24 hours </case_facts> The history around it can be summarised freely; the facts are never paraphrased. For multi-issue sessions, keep one entry per issue so order numbers and amounts never cross over.

Reduce each tool result to the fields that matter for the task before it is added to the conversation, for example in a PostToolUse hook (lesson 1.5). The trimmed result is what accumulates, not the 40-field original.

docs.c: Facts outside the summary · A bigger context window

Anything you would be embarrassed to get wrong (amounts, dates, IDs, promises) lives in a persistent structured block, not in prose history. "Use a model with a larger context window" does not stop summaries from blurring numbers or the middle from being under-used.

Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns. Escalate when the customer asks for a person, when policy is silent or ambiguous, or when the agent cannot make progress; not because of sentiment or a self-reported confidence score. Ask for identifiers instead of guessing between matches.
What you need to know

Trigger Example Action The customer asks for a human "I want to speak to a person, now." Escalate immediately , without first trying to solve it Policy is silent or ambiguous "Do you match a competitor's price?" when policy covers only your own site Escalate; do not invent a policy No meaningful progress Tools keep failing; the problem is outside what the agent can do Escalate with a handoff summary Complexity alone is not a trigger. A long, multi-part case the agent can resolve should be resolved.

- A customer who explicitly asks for a person gets one, even when the fix looks easy. - A customer who is frustrated but has not asked: acknowledge the frustration, offer the resolution if it is within the agent's ability, and escalate if they reiterate that they want a person.

- Sentiment. Annoyed customers often have simple problems; calm customers may need a policy exception. Escalating on negative sentiment sends the wrong cases to humans and keeps the right ones away. - Self-reported confidence. A model's statement of its own confidence is a poor measure of case complexity, so a confidence threshold makes a weak escalation rule.

When get_customer returns three matches for "Sarah Johnson", choosing the one in the same city as the phone's area code is a heuristic guess , and a wrong guess means acting on someone else's account. Ask for an additional identifier (email, account number, an order number) and confirm before acting. The same applies to vague instructions in other scenarios: "clean up this module" with no scope deserves a clarifying question or a proposed scope before broad changes.

Sentiment, confidence scores and "this seems complicated" do not. "Attempt the simple fix, then escalate if needed" is wrong when the customer has explicitly asked for a human. Any heuristic for choosing between matching records (location, most recent, most active) is the distractor. Ask.

Implement error propagation strategies across multi-agent systems. Subagents should recover from transient failures themselves and pass up only what they cannot fix, with the failure type, what was tried, partial results and alternatives. Never hide failures as empty results, and never abort everything for one failure.
What you need to know

docs.h: What the coordinator needs to recover
docs.x: A coordinator can only make a good decision if the failure report says enough. Compare: Report What the coordinator can do "search unavailable" Guess {"failure": "timeout", "attempted": "EU e-bike sales 2025 site:eurostat", "retries": 2, "partial": [3 results], "alternatives": ["try industry body reports", "narrow to Germany"]} Retry differently, switch source, accept partial coverage, or report a gap Structured error context carries the failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, and possible alternatives.

- Access failure : the query did not run (timeout, permission denied). The coordinator must decide whether to retry or work around it. - Valid empty result : the query ran and found nothing. That is information, not an error. Reporting them the same way leads either to pointless retries or to hidden gaps.

1. Silent suppression : returning an empty result as success when the search failed. The report then states conclusions with a gap nobody knows about. 2. Abort on any failure : terminating the whole workflow because one subagent failed throws away all the work that succeeded.

Subagents should retry transient failures themselves (a timeout, a rate-limited call), and propagate only errors they cannot resolve , including what they tried and what they did get. This keeps the coordinator's context for decisions, not for routine retries.

docs.h: Make gaps visible in the output
docs.c: Retry locally, report richly, never hide · "Return empty so the pipeline keeps going"
docs.x: The final synthesis should carry coverage annotations : which findings are well supported (several sources), which rest on one source, and which topic areas have gaps because sources were unavailable. Transient errors are fixed where they occur. Everything else goes up with type, attempt, partial results and alternatives. Keeping the pipeline alive by pretending a failure was an empty success is the silent-suppression anti-pattern.

Coordinator rule. If alternatives exist and the subtopic is central to the question, delegate one alternative. If not, accept the partial results and mark the subtopic thin. Never treat partial failure as complete coverage. 4. Annotation. "Coverage: Regulation and supply chain are well supported (5+ independent sources). Manage context effectively in large codebase exploration. Long explorations degrade as context fills. Write key findings to a scratchpad file, delegate noisy questions to subagents, summarise between phases, use /compact, and export state so a crash does not lose the work.
What you need to know

Hours into an exploration, answers become vague. Asked about the UserAuth class found two hours earlier, the agent describes "typical authentication patterns" instead of the specific methods it read. That is context degradation : the details are buried under thousands of lines of later tool output.

Remedy What it does Scratchpad file The agent writes key findings (class names, method signatures, decisions) to a file such as NOTES.md , and consults it for later questions. The file outlives context limits Subagents for specific questions "Find all test files" or "trace the refund flow's dependencies" goes to a subagent; only its summary returns, and the main agent keeps the high-level picture Summaries between phases Before spawning the next phase's subagents, summarise what the last phase found and inject that summary into their starting context /compact Compresses the conversation so far when context is full of verbose discovery output, so the session can continue State exports Each agent writes its state to a known location; on restart, the coordinator loads a manifest and injects the relevant state into each agent's prompt

Design human review workflows and confidence calibration. An overall accuracy figure can hide weak document types and fields. Check accuracy by segment, keep sampling high-confidence output, calibrate field-level confidence on labelled data, and send reviewers where errors are likely.
What you need to know

"97% accurate" can mean 99.5% on typed invoices and 70% on handwritten receipts, or 99% on totals and 80% on tax IDs. Before reducing human review, break accuracy down by document type and by field , and check every segment meets the bar. Segment Volume Accuracy Typed invoices 70% 99.1% Contracts 10% 96.0% Receipts (photos) 15% 91.5% Handwritten invoices 5% 78.0% Overall this is about 97%, and one segment is far below it.

Once high-confidence extractions skip review, nobody sees their errors. Stratified random sampling keeps a small, regular sample of high-confidence output from every segment going to reviewers. It measures the ongoing error rate and catches new error patterns, such as a supplier changing its layout.

Have the model output a confidence per field , not one per document. Then calibrate the thresholds against a labelled validation set : find the confidence level above which a field is right, say, 99.5% of the time, and use that as the routing threshold. Uncalibrated self-reported confidence is not reliable on its own.

docs.c: Segment, sample, calibrate, route · Approving automation on the aggregate
docs.x: If reviewers can check only 10% of documents, reviewing every tenth in arrival order wastes most of their effort on easy documents. Route instead: - Low-confidence fields. - Documents with ambiguous or contradictory content ( conflict_detected ). - Segments with known weak accuracy. - Plus the small stratified sample of high-confidence output. Validate by segment before automating; keep sampling; set thresholds on labelled data; send review effort where errors are. "97% overall, so stop reviewing high-confidence output" is the trap. The required step is the segment-by-segment check.
